title: My plans: ir a + infinitive
topic: near future with ir a; time expressions
why: After estar + gerund for what's happening right now, this lesson lets you talk about the near future with ir a + infinitive, pensar + infinitive and the present for schedules. With time expressions, you can finally talk about your plans, while you wait for the future and past tenses of level A2.

Voy a cenar: the near future

Just like English “going to”, Spanish talks about plans with the verb “to go” + infinitive: Voy a cenar con Lucía (I'm going to have dinner with Lucía). The structure is the same as in English: ir conjugated, then a (like “to”), then the infinitive.

Personirir a + infinitive
yovoyvoy a trabajar
túvasvas a comer
él, ella, ustedvava a salir
nosotros, nosotrasvamosvamos a viajar
vosotros, vosotrasvaisvais a venir
ellos, ellas, ustedesvanvan a dormir
¿Qué vas a hacer este fin de semana? — Voy a visitar a mis abuelos.What are you going to do this weekend? — I'm going to visit my grandparents.

Negation and pronouns

No goes in front of ir: No voy a salir esta noche. Pronouns can go in front of ir or attach to the end of the infinitive: Lo voy a comprar = Voy a comprarlo. With a reflexive verb: Me voy a duchar = Voy a ducharme.

The English speaker's trap: English says “I'm going to”, with “-ing”, so it's tempting to use estar + gerund (“estoy yendo a cenar”). Don't: for a plan, Spanish uses the simple present of “ir”. And don't drop the a either: “voy cenar” is wrong. And vamos a + infinitive is also used to suggest something, like “let's”: ¡Vamos a ver! (Let's see!)

", "

When? Time expressions

These expressions place your plan in time. They go at the beginning or at the end of the sentence, as in English.

SpanishEnglish
esta tarde / esta nochethis afternoon / tonight
mañanatomorrow
mañana por la mañanatomorrow morning
pasado mañanathe day after tomorrow
este fin de semanathis weekend
la semana que vienenext week
el próximo mes / el mes que vienenext month
el año que vienenext year
dentro de dos díasin two days
dentro de un mesin a month

Watch out for two traps:

  • Mañana means “tomorrow”, and la mañana means “the morning”: so “tomorrow morning” is mañana por la mañana.
  • English “in two days” has two meanings, and Spanish splits them. Two days from now: dentro de dos días. En dos días means “within two days” (the time it takes to do something).
Dentro de tres semanas vamos a ir a Granada.In three weeks, we're going to go to Granada.

Pensar + infinitive: to plan to, to intend to

Pensar (pienso, piensas, piensa, pensamos, pensáis, piensan) followed directly by an infinitive means “to plan to”, “to intend to”. No a here.

Pienso cambiar de trabajo el año que viene.I'm planning to change jobs next year.

Próximo agrees with the noun (English adjectives never change, Spanish ones do): el próximo mes, la próxima semana. Both forms, la próxima semana and la semana que viene, are equally natural.

", "

The present for a fixed schedule

As in English, the present is often used for a future that's already organized: a timetable, an appointment, a schedule. Where English uses “I'm having dinner…” for an arrangement, Spanish simply uses the simple present.

SpanishEnglish
El tren sale a las ocho.The train leaves at eight.
Mañana trabajo hasta las seis.Tomorrow I'm working until six.
El concierto empieza a las nueve.The concert starts at nine.
El sábado ceno con mis padres.On Saturday I'm having dinner with my parents.

Ir a + infinitive rather stresses an intention or something you can see coming: Voy a llamar a Pablo (I've decided to call him), ¡Va a llover! (it's going to rain, look at the sky).

El avión sale a las siete, así que voy a dormir en el aeropuerto.The plane leaves at seven, so I'm going to sleep at the airport.

Talking about your coming weekend

Este fin de semana voy a estar muy ocupada. El sábado por la mañana voy a hacer la compra y por la tarde voy a ver una película con Laura. El domingo como con mi familia.This weekend I'm going to be very busy. On Saturday morning I'm going to do the grocery shopping, and in the afternoon I'm going to see a movie with Laura. On Sunday I'm having lunch with my family.

The Spanish simple future (cenaré, I will have dinner) also exists, but you'll see it later. In everyday life, ir a + infinitive and the present are enough to talk about your plans.
